title: Sisyphus Versus the Flywheel September 1, 2026
author: Chad Aldeman
source: Aldeman On Education (chadaldeman.com), Aldeman On Education (chadaldeman.com),
summary: Chad Aldeman contrasts two competing models that have shaped two decades of urban school reform. The 'Sisyphus Model' concentrates power in a single reform leader installed after a mayoral or state takeover, who pushes achievement up the hill through centralized authority -- only to see gains erode once political winds shift and that leader moves on. The 'Flywheel Model,' by contrast, decentralizes decision-making to individual schools and school networks, with city leaders acting as measurers and gatekeepers: successful schools are allowed to grow and replicate, while chronically low-performing or under-enrolled schools are closed. Aldeman argues the Flywheel Model avoids the Sisyphus Model's dependence on one hero and instead builds improvement into the system's ongoing structure. He frames the piece as an open question -- which model actually produces durable, compounding progress -- rather than a settled verdict, positioning the comparison as a lens for evaluating real-world urban school reform efforts.
points: Aldeman contrasts two dominant models of urban school-system improvement: the 'Sisyphus Model' (centralized mayoral or state takeover under a single reform leader) and the 'Flywheel Model' (decentralized authority pushed down to individual schools and networks).
In the Sisyphus Model, gains are tied to one leader's tenure and tend to erode once that leader departs and political winds shift -- the rock rolls back down the hill.

The Flywheel Model relies on continuous measurement, allowing successful schools to grow and replicate while consistently failing schools close, rather than betting reform on a single charismatic leader.
Aldeman frames the comparison as an open empirical question -- which model actually compounds gains over time -- rather than declaring a clear winner outright.
quotes: In the Sisyphus Model, a city's schools get so bad that the mayor or the state takes over. They appoint some brave new leader who has the authority to concentrate decision-making power, adopt new systems, and bring in new people. With luck, they can push student achievement up the metaphorical hill.

Celebrations ensue, and the hard-charging leader steps out of the picture. But over time, the political winds change, the new systems weaken, old habits return, and the rock starts rolling back down the hill.

Under the Flywheel Model there is no one hero. Instead of centralizing power under a single entity or person, a city devolves much of its decision-making authority to individual schools and school networks.

City leaders measure results, let successful schools grow, and close schools that consistently fail to attract families or produce results. With luck, successful schools grow and replicate, new schools learn from what works, and the lowest-performing and most under-enrolled schools close.

As I describe these models, I have real-world examples in mind. Both models have good stories to tell and have produced genuine successes. But which one would you bet on to make the most progress over time?
